entries.seminar_title: Identification and Optimal Reserve Prices in English Auctions, with an Application to Art
entries.speaker: Kirill Ponomarev
entries.abstract: We develop a partial-identification approach for English auctions with private values, auction-level heterogeneity unobserved by the analyst, and a potentially unknown number of bidders. Our framework permits restrictions on dependence among bidders' valuations away from the extreme cases of independent private values and perfect correlation, yielding sharp and informative bounds on the distribution of the highest valuation and the seller's expected profit. We formulate reserve-price choice as a minimax-regret problem and derive tractable solutions to two relaxations of this problem. We apply our method to a new dataset covering more than 3,500 lots auctioned by Christie's and Sotheby's. For modern art sold in New York City with pre-sale estimates between $1 million and $10 million, we find that setting the reserve price 37 percent above the sellers projected value from retaining an unsold lot increases expected profit by approximately $150,000 to $489,000 per lot, equivalent to 27 to 87 percent of average realized profit.

entries.seminar_title: The Female Labor Supply Constraints of Spousal Jealousy: Experimental Evidence from India
entries.speaker: Kailash Rajah
entries.abstract: This study presents evidence from two field experiments studying the role of spousal jealousy in constraining married women’s employment. In a first experiment (N=1,400), I randomize married women in India to receive a two-week job in either a mixed or women-only workplace. Women randomized to the women-only workplace are 46 percent more likely to spontaneously apply for a job (13 percentage points) and 31 percent more likely to attend the workplace (6 percentage points). A cross-randomized safety treatment suggests that workplace safety is not the main mechanism. Instead, the treatment effects are significantly stronger among women who report having more jealous and controlling husbands. In a second experiment (N=210), I directly test for a spousal jealousy mechanism by measuring whether women are more willing to interact with a male colleague if their husbands can monitor the interaction. I offer women a job that comes with a compulsory online peer support program and give them the option to forgo 20-35% of their salary to guarantee that the peer they are matched with will be a woman rather than a man. Fifty-three percent of women pay for the female peer when these remote interactions are one-on-one, but this drops to 34 percent once their husbands have the option of joining and can therefore monitor the conversations. One-third of households still pay for a female peer even if the mentoring simply involves watching pre-recorded videos of the peer, suggesting even the most innocuous interactions are enough to raise jealousy concerns.
